title: When All Rollouts Fail: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning

paper.title: When All Rollouts Fail: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) derives its learning signal from binary rewards via on-policy exploration and becomes a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning of large language models. Yet it faces a learning cliff on problems beyond model’s current ability: when every rollout fails, the samples reveal nothing about a correct solution, and group-relative estimators (e.g., GRPO, RLOO) collapse the update to zero advantage. Expert trajectories offer a remedy, but they are incompatible with the current policy and often lie in the student’s low-probability regions, so the surviving updates demand large parameter shifts and decay into surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning. We argue that a useful learning signal on hard problems must be both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current policy.
We propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning ( PICO ), which performs distribution-constrained joint decoding: expert data guides decoding at the token level while preserving the student’s relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism confines the sampling distribution under a finite divergence budget, yielding trajectories that are verified and policy-compatible by construction. These trajectories are optimized jointly with on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that mitigates their distribution mismatch via importance sampling. Experiments across reasoning diverse datasets and agentic benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs) ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Jaech et al., 2024 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , demonstrating strong effectiveness in enhancing reasoning capabilities across domains such as mathematics, coding, and agentic tasks ( Dong et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . RLVR enables LLMs to learn directly from verifiable reward feedback on trajectories generated through on-policy exploration, yielding substantial and generalizable performance gains ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . However, this reliance on successful exploration creates a learning cliff on challenging problems beyond the model’s current capabilities: when all sampled rollouts fail, the policy receives no positive reward signal ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Yue et al., 2025 ) . This issue is particularly acute for methods based on group-relative advantage estimation (e.g., GRPO) ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) , as all-zero-reward groups cause the estimated advantages to collapse to zero, leaving no informative learning signal to drive futher improvement on these problems. A natural remedy is to leverage expert data, which offer a promising way to overcome this exploration bottleneck and are increasingly used to supplement online RL training. Typically generated by human experts or stronger models, expert trajectories expose the student to high-quality reasoning paths and provide informative learning signals. Yet these trajectories are not necessarily compatible with the current policy and often fall within low-probability regions under its distribution. Existing methods utilize such trajectories in three main ways. Some use them as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) targets alongside RL training ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . When these trajectories lie in low-probability regions under the current policy, directly fitting them can induce excessive policy drift and result in surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning ( Yan et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches incorporate expert trajectories into rollout groups as off-policy samples to recover informative learning signals ( Yan et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . The distributional mismatch between these off-policy trajectories and on-policy rollouts can distort the resulting learning signals and destabilize optimization ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Setlur et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . A further line of work ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Qu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) leverages expert trajectories indirectly, using them to construct prefixes or hints that guide subsequent exploration and generation. Although the resulting continuations are generated by the current policy, they are conditioned on intermediate states that the policy may not be able to reach on its own from the original prompt ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Qu et al., 2026 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) . This creates privileged-context dependence: once the guidance is removed, the model may struggle to reproduce the full reasoning process. Collectively, these limitations reveal a fundamental trade-off: an effective learning signal on challenging problems must come from trajectories that are both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current student policy. Although expert data can provide verifiably correct trajectories, naively incorporating them may sacrifice policy compatibility by pulling the policy toward behaviors that lie far outside its current distribution, ultimately undermining stable and effective policy improvement. To address this challenge, we propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning ( PICO ), which uses distribution-constrained joint decoding to recover positive learning signals from off-policy trajectories while explicitly controlling the induced distribution shift. Specifically, joint decoding constructs the next-token candidate set by intersecting high-probability tokens predicted by a teacher conditioned on expert data with those predicted by the student, thereby restricting sampling to candidates favored by both models. In this way, the teacher provides token-level guidance to improve rollout accuracy, while sampling according to the student’s relative probabilities preserves its own preferences. To further constrain the joint sampling distribution within a finite divergence budget, we introduce a dynamic top- k k mechanism that adaptively adjusts the teacher’s candidate set. Finally, the resulting trajectories verified for correctness are optimized alongside on-policy rollouts through a mixed-behavior objective. As illustrated in Figure 1 , PICO activates joint decoding only for all-failure groups, preserving standard on-policy optimization whenever student exploration already yields positive rewards. Figure 4 further shows that joint decoding recovers verified, positive-reward trajectories in up to 80% of all-failure groups, thereby restoring informative learning signals where standard on-policy sampling yields none. Extensive experiments across mathematics and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and existing expert-guided baselines. Further evaluations on agentic tasks establish its generalizability beyond conventional reasoning settings. Comprehensive ablation studies validate the effectiveness of its key components and confirm the importance of explicitly controlling the trade-off between rollout quality and student-policy proximity. In summary, our main contributions are threefold: • We identify a fundamental trade-off between rollout quality and student-policy proximity when incorporating offline expert information into RLVR. • We introduce PICO , which combines distribution-constrained joint decoding with failure-triggered mixed-behavior optimization to generate and learn from verified, policy-compatible trajectories. • Extensive experiments on mathematics, general reasoning, and agentic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of PICO .

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: In this section, we detail the design and implementation of PICO . As illustrated in Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 , the framework consists of two components: distribution-constrained joint decoding and mixed-behavior policy optimization. First, distribution-constrained joint decoding combines the token-level preferences of the teacher and student to generate rollouts, with a dynamic top- k k mechanism adaptively balancing teacher guidance and distribution shift. Second, mixed-behavior policy optimization learns from the resulting trajectories using importance-sampling (IS) ratios to account for the mismatch between the joint-decoding policy and the student policy.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Models and Datasets. In our main experiments, we consider three student policies with different model scales and instruction-tuning configurations: Qwen3-4B-Base, Qwen3-8B-Base, and Qwen3-4B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . We use Qwen3-4B-Instruct specifically for the agentic-task experiments. Across all settings, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, conditioned on expert solutions, serves as the teacher model. For mathematical and general reasoning tasks, we use DAPO-Math-17K ( Yu et al., 2026 ) as the training set, which contains a large collection of challenging problems paired with high-quality expert demonstrations. For agentic tasks, we conduct experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, two widely used interactive reasoning benchmarks. Baselines. We compare PICO against GRPO and three representative off-policy methods , as well as a self-distillation baseline. Specifically, LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2025 ) combines on-policy rollouts with off-policy demonstrations through mixed-policy GRPO and regularized policy shaping; Prefix-RFT ( Huang et al., 2026 ) constructs hybrid trajectories by pairing prefixes sampled from expert demonstrations with policy-generated continuations; and ReLIFT ( Ma et al., 2026 ) interleaves reinforcement learning with targeted online supervised fine-tuning on challenging problems. We additionally compare with RLRT ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , a self-distillation method that uses reversed teacher signals to emphasize student-preferred tokens in verified successful trajectories. Training Details. For a fair comparison, we use the same training configuration for all RL methods. We remove the KL regularization term by setting β = 0 \beta=0 and omit standard-deviation normalization in the advantage computation to avoid implicitly reweighting problems according to their within-group reward variance. We fix the total rollout group size at 8 for every query. For PICO and all off-policy baselines, each mixed group consists of 7 on-policy trajectories and 1 off-policy trajectory. We use a global training batch size of 128, a PPO mini-batch size of 64, and a maximum response length of 20,480 20{,}480 tokens. Following DAPO, we adopt asymmetric clipping with ϵ high = 0.28 \epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}=0.28 and ϵ low = 0.20 \epsilon_{\mathrm{low}}=0.20 . The complete training configuration is provided in Appendix C.1 . Evaluations. Following prior work, we evaluate primarily on four widely used and challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks: AIME 2025, AIME 2026, HMMT 2026, and MATH-500. During evaluation, we set the sampling temperature to 0.6 0.6 and the maximum response length to 20,480 20{,}480 tokens. To reduce the effect of sampling variance, we independently sample 16 responses for each problem and report the average accuracy across these samples (avg@16). To assess out-of-distribution generalization beyond the mathematics-focused training domain, we additionally evaluate on GPQA-Diamond and Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE). sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: Performance Comparison. As shown in Table 1 , PICO consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across both model scales. It improves the average score over GRPO by 4.1 4.1 percentage points with Qwen3-4B-Base and by 3.6 3.6 points with Qwen3-8B-Base, while outperforming the strongest competing method by 2.2 2.2 and 1.8 1.8 points, respectively. The gains are particularly pronounced on challenging benchmarks such as AIME26 and HMMT26, supporting our claim that PICO enables effective learning from difficult problems that frequently produce all-incorrect rollout groups. Moreover, the consistent improvements on GPQA-Diamond and HLE demonstrate that the learned reasoning capability generalizes beyond the mathematics-focused training distribution. Since the teacher is unavailable during evaluation, these gains reflect improvements internalized by the student rather than reliance on privileged guidance. Training Dynamics. Figure 2 shows that PICO maintains higher training rewards and consistently fewer solve-none questions than GRPO and LUFFY across both model scales. While the baselines tend to plateau after the initial stage, PICO continues to improve, indicating that failure-triggered joint decoding converts otherwise uninformative all-incorrect groups into useful learning signals. PICO also produces longer responses, which, together with the higher verified rewards and lower solve-none counts, suggests more sustained reasoning on difficult problems. Overall, these results show that PICO improves difficult-problem exploration without compromising training stability. Additional analyses in Appendix B.2 and Fig. 4 show that joint decoding consistently rescues questions for which all student self-sampled trajectories fail, thereby restoring effective learning signals for otherwise uninformative groups.

sections.heading: 4.4 Ablation Study
sections.text: We analyze the contribution of each component of PICO . As shown in Table 3 , the results highlight the importance of maintaining compatibility between guided trajectories and the student policy. Directly sampling from the teacher without joint decoding introduces the largest behavior mismatch and yields the weakest ablation result, reducing the average score from 37.2 % 37.2\% to 33.8 % 33.8\% . The fixed- k k variants further reveal a trade-off between teacher guidance and student compatibility. Increasing k k retains more student-compatible tokens but weakens the selectivity of teacher guidance, potentially reducing rollout accuracy. As long as the candidate set remains sufficiently accurate, increasing k k improves learning, as evidenced by the gain from k = 5 k=5 to k = 10 k=10 . However, further increasing k k to 20 20 weakens teacher guidance and slightly reduces performance, making k = 10 k=10 the best fixed setting. In contrast, our dynamic top- k k strategy adapts the candidate set at each decoding step according to the retained student probability mass, achieving a better balance and the highest average score of 37.2 % 37.2\% . Finally, removing the off-policy importance-sampling ratio reduces performance to 35.3 % 35.3\% , confirming the importance of explicitly accounting for the remaining behavior-policy mismatch during optimization.

sections.heading: 5.1 On- and Off-Policy Learning
sections.text: Recent studies show that on-policy optimization is fundamentally bounded by the current policy’s exploration capacity, often causing learning to stall on challenging problems ( Yue et al., 2025 ) . To overcome this exploration bottleneck, a growing line of work incorporates off-policy expert trajectories into RLVR training ( Dong et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2025 ) combines expert demonstrations with on-policy rollouts through mixed-policy optimization, while ReLIFT ( Ma et al., 2026 ) interleaves reinforcement learning with supervised fine-tuning on high-quality solutions to challenging problems. SRFT and Chord further unifies supervised learning from expert demonstrations and reinforcement learning from self-generated rollouts within a single training stage ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . However, because expert trajectories may lie in low-probability regions under the current student policy, directly optimizing on them can induce substantial distribution mismatch, potentially leading to excessive policy drift and unstable optimization ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Setlur et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, PICO uses expert trajectories to guide distribution-constrained joint decoding, producing successful rollouts that remain compatible with the student policy.

sections.heading: 5.2 Expert-Guided Exploration and Decoding
sections.text: Rather than directly optimizing on off-policy demonstrations, another line of work uses expert information to guide rollout generation ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Prefix-RFT ( Huang et al., 2026 ) conditions rollouts on prefixes sampled from expert demonstrations, while BREAD and StepHint use expert-derived prefixes or intermediate hints to steer exploration toward promising reasoning states ( Zhang et al., 2026d ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . OC-GRPO ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) further applies importance sampling ratio to account for the mismatch between guided rollouts and the original unguided policy. Although these methods facilitate successful exploration, injecting guidance into the rollout context may teach the student to continue from expert-induced states without learning how to reach those states independently from the original prompt ( Qu et al., 2026 ; Ross et al., 2011 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . A related line of work combines or contrasts the token distributions of models with different capabilities to steer generation toward higher-quality outputs ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Dekoninck et al., 2024 ) . The effectiveness of these methods motivates us to incorporate teacher guidance at the token level. Accordingly, PICO employs distribution-constrained joint decoding to construct policy-compatible trajectories.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced PICO , a policy-compatible reinforcement learning framework for overcoming the exploration bottleneck of RLVR on challenging problems. PICO leverages expert data to generate verified trajectories while controlling their deviation from the student policy, and selectively incorporates these trajectories into all-failure groups to restore informative learning signals. Extensive experiments across mathematical reasoning, general reasoning, and agentic tasks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and representative expert-guided baselines across different model scales, without requiring teacher guidance at inference time. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component. Overall, our results highlight policy compatibility as a key principle for effectively incorporating expert knowledge into RLVR, providing a practical approach to improving models beyond the limits of unaided on-policy exploration.

sections.text: Question Rescue through Joint Decoding. Figure 4 directly illustrates how joint decoding recovers learning signals from questions that are entirely unsolved by student self-sampling. Across training, joint decoding rescues approximately 80 % 80\% and 76 % 76\% of these questions for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on mathematical reasoning tasks, respectively, substantially reducing the number of all-incorrect groups. It also rescues 36 % 36\% of the failed questions on ALFWorld, despite the greater difficulty of long-horizon interaction. These results confirm that joint decoding enables the policy to obtain successful trajectories on problems beyond the reach of its current self-exploration, thereby converting otherwise uninformative groups into effective training signals. sections.heading: Mathematical Reasoning Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate mathematical reasoning on AIME 2025, AIME 2026, HMMT 2026, and MATH500. AIME 2025 and AIME 2026 each contain 30 problems drawn from the corresponding AIME I and AIME II competitions. These problems require exact numerical answers and cover algebra, geometry, combinatorics, and number theory. HMMT 2026 contains 33 problems from the February 2026 Harvard–MIT Mathematics Tournament and provides a complementary evaluation of advanced competition-level mathematical reasoning. MATH-500 is a widely used subset of the MATH test set comprising 500 problems across seven mathematical subjects and a range of difficulty levels. Compared with the recent competition benchmarks, MATH-500 provides broader coverage of mathematical topics and evaluates performance on a larger and more diverse problem set. Since our reasoning models are trained on DAPO-Math-17K, we treat these three competition-mathematics benchmarks as in-domain evaluations.

sections.heading: Out-of-domain Reasoning Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate cross-domain generalization on GPQA-Diamond and Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE). GPQA-Diamond contains 198 expert-written, graduate-level multiple-choice questions, primarily covering physics, chemistry, and biology. The full HLE benchmark comprises 2,500 expert-level questions spanning more than 100 academic and professional subjects. We use its text-only subset, which contains 500 questions and excludes items that require multimodal inputs. These benchmarks differ substantially from the mathematics-focused training distribution and therefore assess whether the reasoning capabilities acquired during training transfer to previously unseen domains.

sections.heading: Agentic Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate agentic reasoning on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld using Qwen3-4B-Instruct. ALFWorld is a text-based interactive benchmark in which an agent must complete household tasks by interpreting observations and executing sequences of admissible actions. Following the standard evaluation protocol, we evaluate on 140 task instances from the valid-seen split and 134 task instances from the valid-unseen split. ScienceWorld is an interactive text environment centered on elementary-science reasoning. It comprises 30 task types across 10 scientific topics, instantiated into 1,819 task variations. These tasks require the agent to explore the environment, manipulate objects, and complete multi-step scientific procedures. For both benchmarks, each rollout corresponds to a complete interaction episode, and we use the environment-provided task-completion signal to determine success.

sections.heading: Evaluation Hyperparameters.
sections.text: For all reasoning benchmarks, we independently sample 16 responses per problem and report both avg@16 and pass@16. We use a sampling temperature of 0.6 0.6 , top- p p of 1 1 , top- k k of − 1 -1 , and a maximum response length of 20,480 20{,}480 tokens. We apply the same prompt template, answer extractor, and verifier to all methods. For ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, we use a sampling temperature of 1 and a maximum of 20 interaction steps per episode. We evaluate each task instance over 8 episode(s) and report the mean episode success rate. During all evaluations, the student operates independently from the original task input without expert solutions, teacher predictions, or joint decoding.

sections.heading: Appendix D Prompts
sections.text: we present the prompts used for mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks. The student prompt contains only the original task information and the interaction context available under the target policy. The teacher receives the same task context together with privileged guidance derived from off-policy data. For mathematical reasoning, this guidance is an expert solution associated with the training problem. For ALFWorld, it is a known-correct expert trajectory, which the teacher aligns with the current observation and action history to identify a suitable next action. The off-policy data is never included in the student’s prompt or generated context. Instead, the teacher uses it only to produce token-level predictions during joint decoding, while the student distribution determines the relative sampling probabilities over the retained candidate tokens. This design incorporates information from successful off-policy solutions without training the student directly on their full trajectories or exposing privileged information at inference time.

Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory Abstract Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) derives its learning signal from binary rewards via on-policy exploration and becomes a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning of large language models. Yet it faces a learning cliff on problems beyond model’s current ability: when every rollout fails, the samples reveal nothing about a correct solution, and group-relative estimators (e.g., GRPO, RLOO) collapse the update to zero advantage. Expert trajectories offer a remedy, but they are incompatible with the current policy and often lie in the student’s low-probability regions, so the surviving updates demand large parameter shifts and decay into surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning. We argue that a useful learning signal on hard problems must be both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current policy. We propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning ( PICO ), which performs distribution-constrained joint decoding: expert data guides decoding at the token level while preserving the student’s relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism confines the sampling distribution under a finite divergence budget, yielding trajectories that are verified and policy-compatible by construction. These trajectories are optimized jointly with on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that mitigates their distribution mismatch via importance sampling. Experiments across reasoning diverse datasets and agentic benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs) ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Jaech et al., 2024 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , demonstrating strong effectiveness in enhancing reasoning capabilities across domains such as mathematics, coding, and agentic tasks ( Dong et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . RLVR enables LLMs to learn directly from verifiable reward feedback on trajectories generated through on-policy exploration, yielding substantial and generalizable performance gains ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . However, this reliance on successful exploration creates a learning cliff on challenging problems beyond the model’s current capabilities: when all sampled rollouts fail, the policy receives no positive reward signal ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Yue et al., 2025 ) . This issue is particularly acute for methods based on group-relative advantage estimation (e.g., GRPO) ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) , as all-zero-reward groups cause the estimated advantages to collapse to zero, leaving no informative learning signal to drive futher improvement on these problems. A natural remedy is to leverage expert data, which offer a promising way to overcome this exploration bottleneck and are increasingly used to supplement online RL training. Typically generated by human experts or stronger models, expert trajectories expose the student to high-quality reasoning paths and provide informative learning signals. Yet these trajectories are not necessarily compatible with the current policy and often fall within low-probability regions under its distribution. Existing methods utilize such trajectories in three main ways. Some use them as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) targets alongside RL training ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . When these trajectories lie in low-probability regions under the current policy, directly fitting them can induce excessive policy drift and result in surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning ( Yan et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches incorporate expert trajectories into rollout groups as off-policy samples to recover informative learning signals ( Yan et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . The distributional mismatch between these off-policy trajectories and on-policy rollouts can distort the resulting learning signals and destabilize optimization ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Setlur et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . A further line of work ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Qu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) leverages expert trajectories indirectly, using them to construct prefixes or hints that guide subsequent exploration and generation. Although the resulting continuations are generated by the current policy, they are conditioned on intermediate states that the policy may not be able to reach on its own from the original prompt ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Qu et al., 2026 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) . This creates privileged-context dependence: once the guidance is removed, the model may struggle to reproduce the full reasoning process. Collectively, these limitations reveal a fundamental trade-off: an effective learning signal on challenging problems must come from trajectories that are both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current student policy. Although expert data can provide verifiably correct trajectories, naively incorporating them may sacrifice policy compatibility by pulling the policy toward behaviors that lie far outside its current distribution, ultimately undermining stable and effective policy improvement. To address this challenge, we propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning ( PICO ), which uses distribution-constrained joint decoding to recover positive learning signals from off-policy trajectories while explicitly controlling the induced distribution shift. Specifically, joint decoding constructs the next-token candidate set by intersecting high-probability tokens predicted by a teacher conditioned on expert data with those predicted by the student, thereby restricting sampling to candidates favored by both models. In this way, the teacher provides token-level guidance to improve rollout accuracy, while sampling according to the student’s relative probabilities preserves its own preferences. To further constrain the joint sampling distribution within a finite divergence budget, we introduce a dynamic top- k k mechanism that adaptively adjusts the teacher’s candidate set. Finally, the resulting trajectories verified for correctness are optimized alongside on-policy rollouts through a mixed-behavior objective. As illustrated in Figure 1 , PICO activates joint decoding only for all-failure groups, preserving standard on-policy optimization whenever student exploration already yields positive rewards. Figure 4 further shows that joint decoding recovers verified, positive-reward trajectories in up to 80% of all-failure groups, thereby restoring informative learning signals where standard on-policy sampling yields none. Extensive experiments across mathematics and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and existing expert-guided baselines. Further evaluations on agentic tasks establish its generalizability beyond conventional reasoning settings. Comprehensive ablation studies validate the effectiveness of its key components and confirm the importance of explicitly controlling the trade-off between rollout quality and student-policy proximity. In summary, our main contributions are threefold: • We identify a fundamental trade-off between rollout quality and student-policy proximity when incorporating offline expert information into RLVR. • We introduce PICO , which combines distribution-constrained joint decoding with failure-triggered mixed-behavior optimization to generate and learn from verified, policy-compatible trajectories. • Extensive experiments on mathematics, general reasoning, and agentic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of PICO . 2 Preliminaries Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards. To overcome this exploration bottleneck, a growing line of work incorporates off-policy expert trajectories into RLVR training ( Dong et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2025 ) combines expert demonstrations with on-policy rollouts through mixed-policy optimization, while ReLIFT ( Ma et al., 2026 ) interleaves reinforcement learning with supervised fine-tuning on high-quality solutions to challenging problems. SRFT and Chord further unifies supervised learning from expert demonstrations and reinforcement learning from self-generated rollouts within a single training stage ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . However, because expert trajectories may lie in low-probability regions under the current student policy, directly optimizing on them can induce substantial distribution mismatch, potentially leading to excessive policy drift and unstable optimization ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Setlur et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, PICO uses expert trajectories to guide distribution-constrained joint decoding, producing successful rollouts that remain compatible with the student policy. 5.2 Expert-Guided Exploration and Decoding Rather than directly optimizing on off-policy demonstrations, another line of work uses expert information to guide rollout generation ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Prefix-RFT ( Huang et al., 2026 ) conditions rollouts on prefixes sampled from expert demonstrations, while BREAD and StepHint use expert-derived prefixes or intermediate hints to steer exploration toward promising reasoning states ( Zhang et al., 2026d ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . OC-GRPO ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) further applies importance sampling ratio to account for the mismatch between guided rollouts and the original unguided policy. Although these methods facilitate successful exploration, injecting guidance into the rollout context may teach the student to continue from expert-induced states without learning how to reach those states independently from the original prompt ( Qu et al., 2026 ; Ross et al., 2011 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . A related line of work combines or contrasts the token distributions of models with different capabilities to steer generation toward higher-quality outputs ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Dekoninck et al., 2024 ) . The effectiveness of these methods motivates us to incorporate teacher guidance at the token level. Accordingly, PICO employs distribution-constrained joint decoding to construct policy-compatible trajectories. 6 Conclusion In this work, we introduced PICO , a policy-compatible reinforcement learning framework for overcoming the exploration bottleneck of RLVR on challenging problems. PICO leverages expert data to generate verified trajectories while controlling their deviation from the student policy, and selectively incorporates these trajectories into all-failure groups to restore informative learning signals. Extensive experiments across mathematical reasoning, general reasoning, and agentic tasks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and representative expert-guided baselines across different model scales, without requiring teacher guidance at inference time. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component. Overall, our results highlight policy compatibility as a key principle for effectively incorporating expert knowledge into RLVR, providing a practical approach to improving models beyond the limits of unaided on-policy exploration.
